title: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
summary: Why tiny benchmarks report impossible or misleading times: dead code, folding and hoisting, warm caches, noise, and layout or JIT bias, plus the harness tools and statistics that fix each.
outcomes: Explain how dead-code elimination, constant folding and loop hoisting make a benchmark time nothing
Use DoNotOptimize and ClobberMemory correctly and spot a hoisted or folded benchmark
Predict how working set size and warm versus cold caches change a measured time
Compute a 95% confidence interval from repeated runs and judge whether two versions differ
Explain measurement bias from memory layout and JIT profiles, and how randomization and forks counter it

lessons.title: When the optimizer deletes the code you meant to time

blocks.md:
A **microbenchmark** times a tiny piece of code, such as one function call or one hash lookup, by running it many times in a loop and dividing the elapsed time by the number of runs. It is the right tool for questions like "is this division slower than that multiply?".

The trap: the benchmark is compiled by the same optimizer you met in the prerequisite course. That optimizer is allowed to rewrite your loop in any way that keeps the program's *visible* behavior the same. A timing loop whose result nobody reads has no visible behavior at all.

blocks.caption: A naive benchmark. compute squares d and divides by 42, ten times in a row.

blocks.prompt: Compile this with `clang++ -O2` and run it with n = 100 million on a laptop. Ten multiply-and-divide steps per call. Roughly what does it report per call?
blocks.reveal: About **0.000 ns** per call (median of 5 runs on an Apple M5 Pro). Not fast: zero. The compiler removed the whole loop, so the timer measured two back-to-back clock reads. A result that is faster than one clock cycle (well under 1 ns on a GHz chip) means you measured nothing.

blocks.title: How -O2 turns bench_wrong into a single ret

nodes.label:
compute body
10 x (d = d x d / 42)

scenes.caption: As written: n calls to compute, each doing ten multiplies and ten divides. This is the work you think you are timing.
Step 1, inlining: compute is static and tiny, so its body is copied into the loop. The call disappears and the optimizer now sees the whole computation in one function.

labels.loop:
for i < n:
  d = x; 10 x (d = d x d / 42)

scenes.caption: Step 2, dead-code elimination: d is never stored, returned or printed, and the arithmetic has no side effects. Code whose result is unused is dead, so it is deleted.
Step 3, an empty loop has no effect either, so it goes too. The x86-64 output for the loop function is literally one ret instruction; only the two clock reads around it remain.

blocks.md:
That compiler output is real: clang -O2 for x86-64 compiles `bench_wrong` (with the timer calls moved out) to just `ret`. JMH, the Java benchmark harness, opens its dead-code sample the same way: "The downfall of many benchmarks is Dead-Code Elimination (DCE)".

The sibling trap is **constant folding**: if the inputs are known at compile time, the optimizer computes the answer itself. Write `s += compute(42)` instead and clang notices that 42 x 42 / 42 = 42, so every call returns 42. The whole loop becomes `imul ecx, edi, 42`: one multiply of n by 42.

blocks.caption: The result is used, so nothing is dead, but a known input let the compiler skip every call.

blocks.md: Misconception: "returning or summing the result is enough". Using the output defeats dead-code elimination, but not constant folding. The input must also come from somewhere the compiler cannot see through. JMH's constant-folding sample says to read inputs from non-final fields of a state object, and warns against making them `final` even when your IDE suggests it.

A benchmark measures real work only if (1) its result is observably consumed and (2) its inputs are unknown at compile time. A time per operation below one CPU cycle is proof that one of these failed.

blocks.question: A colleague's benchmark reports 0.25 ns per call for a function that parses a 40-byte string. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The parser is vectorized and handles many bytes per cycle
The compiler removed or folded the work, so the loop no longer parses anything
The timer has 1 ns resolution, so the number is rounded down
The string fits in L1 cache, so parsing is nearly free
blocks.explain: Parsing 40 bytes cannot finish in about one clock cycle, even with vector instructions and a warm L1 cache. Timer resolution is not the issue either: the total time is divided by many iterations. An impossible per-call time almost always means the result was unused (dead code) or the input was a compile-time constant (folding).

blocks.question: Which change alone stops clang from folding `bench_fold` into one multiply?
options: Returning s from the function
Marking compute as inline
Passing the input as a function parameter whose value the compiler cannot see, instead of the literal 42
Increasing n to 10 billion
blocks.explain: bench_fold already returns s, and that did not help: folding needs only that the input be known. An inline hint changes nothing (compute was already inlined). A larger n changes the multiply, not the strategy. An unknown input stops the folding, but clang still runs compute once before the loop and multiplies by n (hoisting, next lesson).

lessons.title: DoNotOptimize, loop hoisting and who owns the loop

blocks.md: Benchmark libraries give you tools to make work observable without adding real cost. In Google Benchmark, `benchmark::DoNotOptimize(v)` is an empty inline assembly statement. The compiler cannot look inside asm, so it must assume the asm reads `v`, may change it, and (because of the `"memory"` clobber) may read or write any memory. No machine instruction is emitted; only the optimizer's knowledge is erased.

blocks.caption: Simplified from Google Benchmark's utils.h (clang branch). The real header has overloads for const values, large types and MSVC.

blocks.prompt: You fix the lesson 1 benchmark by adding only `int r = compute(x); DoNotOptimize(r);` inside the loop, with x a function parameter. Does it now time ten multiply-divide steps per iteration?
blocks.reveal: No. It reports about **0.231 ns** per iteration, versus **3.12 ns** for a correct version (medians of 5 runs, Apple M5 Pro). The result is consumed, but x never changes inside the loop, so compute(x) is **loop-invariant**: the compiler computes it once before the loop (loop-invariant code motion, or hoisting) and the loop only stores the same r n times. The x86-64 output shows all ten multiply-shift steps above the loop label, and a loop body of one store.

scenes.caption: Dead code: the loop was deleted, so the measured time per iteration rounds to 0.000 ns.
DoNotOptimize(r) only: the work was hoisted out of the loop. 0.231 ns is the cost of a store plus the loop counter, not of compute.

DoNotOptimize(x) before and DoNotOptimize(r) after: the compiler must reload x every iteration, so compute really runs. 3.12 ns, 13.5 times the hoisted number. Measured on one Apple M5 Pro with clang -O2; your machine will differ.

blocks.title: What each DoNotOptimize forbids

scenes.caption: x is an ordinary local initialized to 41. Without help, the compiler knows its value at every point in the function.
Inside the harness loop, DoNotOptimize(x) claims an unknown asm read and rewrote x. From here on the compiler must treat x as an unknown value in a register or memory.
compute(x) now has an unknown input, so it can neither be folded to a constant nor hoisted above the loop: the previous iteration's asm might have changed x.
DoNotOptimize(r) claims the asm reads r, so r is live and the ten steps that produce it cannot be deleted as dead code.
The harness repeats the body for as many iterations as it decides (next figure) and divides the elapsed time by that count.

blocks.md:
Two more rules from the Google Benchmark user guide:

- `DoNotOptimize(expr)` "does not prevent optimizations on `<expr>` in any way". `DoNotOptimize(foo(0))` can still become `DoNotOptimize(42)`. Store the result in a local, and escape the inputs too.
- `ClobberMemory()` forces pending writes to memory to happen. It acts as a compiler-only barrier: without it, a `v.push_back(42)` into a vector nobody reads could be removed. Memory owned by a local object must first be escaped with `DoNotOptimize` on its pointer.

**Who owns the loop.** Writing your own repeat loop inside a benchmark (call the function 1000 times, divide by 1000) hands the optimizer a loop it can merge. JMH's loops sample does exactly this with `s += x + y` and shows the reported cost per addition falling as the repeat count grows, eventually to "1/20 ns, well beyond what hardware can actually do". In C the same thing happens: clang compiles a `reps` loop of `s += x + y` into one `lea` and one `imul`, computing (x + y) x reps with no loop at all.

JMH owns the loop for you. In Google Benchmark the `for (auto _ : state)` loop lives in your function, so the compiler sees it: escape inputs and outputs on every iteration.

blocks.title: How Google Benchmark grows the iteration count

scenes.caption: Simplified model: every iteration costs exactly 3 ns. The runner starts with 1 iteration. 3 ns is far below 10% of the 0.5 s default minimum time, so the next try uses 10 times as many.
Each try under 50 ms (10% of 0.5 s) multiplies the count by 10. Every try is a full timed batch; only the batch total is divided by the count.
1e8 iterations take 0.3 s: above 10% of the minimum, so the runner extrapolates instead: multiplier = 0.5 x 1.4 / 0.3 = 2.33, aiming 40% past the minimum time.
2.33e8 iterations take 0.7 s, at least 0.5 s, so this batch is reported. Total time spent getting there: 1.03 s. Rule read from benchmark_runner.cc; the minimum time is set with --benchmark_min_time.

blocks.md: Read the assembly of anything surprising. `objdump -d`, `perf annotate` or Compiler Explorer will show in a minute whether your work is inside the timed loop, above it, or gone. It is how the hoisting bug above was found.

blocks.question: A Google Benchmark loop does `auto h = hash(key); benchmark::DoNotOptimize(h);` where key is a std::string built once before the loop. The result looks too fast. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add benchmark::ClobberMemory() after the hash
Call DoNotOptimize on key (or its data) inside the loop as well, so the hash cannot be hoisted
Wrap the call in your own loop of 1000 and divide by 1000
Run with --benchmark_repetitions=10
blocks.explain: The output is consumed, but the input never changes, so hash(key) is loop-invariant and may be computed once. Escaping the input each iteration forces recomputation. ClobberMemory only flushes pending stores; an inner loop gives the optimizer more to merge; repetitions repeat the same wrong number.

blocks.question: Why does JMH discourage writing your own repeat loop inside a @Benchmark method?
options: Loops in Java cannot be JIT compiled
The optimizer can unroll the loop and hoist or merge the repeated operation, so cost per operation shrinks with the repeat count
JMH cannot count loop iterations, so the result is reported per call instead of per operation
Loops prevent the method from being inlined into the harness
blocks.explain: JMHSample_11_Loops shows the perceived per-operation cost falling as the repeat count grows, to about 1/20 ns per addition, because the loop is unrolled and pipelined and the operation is hoisted. @OperationsPerInvocation does the division correctly; the measured code is what is wrong.

lessons.title: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production

blocks.md:
Recall from the cache hierarchy course: a load is fast when its cache line is already in a nearby cache and slow when it must come from DRAM. A microbenchmark runs the same code on the same data millions of times in a row. After the first iteration, everything it touches, code and data, sits in the fastest cache that can hold it, and the branch predictor has seen the same path over and over.

In a real program, the function runs between other work that evicts its data. So the benchmark answers "how fast is this when everything is hot?", which may not be the question you have.

Ulrich Drepper's [What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory](https://people.freebsd.org/~lstewart/articles/cpumemory.pdf) quotes the access costs Intel lists for a Pentium M: about 3 cycles for L1d, 14 for L2 and 240 for main memory. Old numbers, but the ratios (L1 to DRAM is around two orders of magnitude) still describe modern chips. The figure below turns them into a simplified model of average cost per random access as the **working set** (bytes the loop touches repeatedly) grows.

blocks.caption: Average cycles per uniformly random access to a working set of W bytes, with an L1 of C1 and an L2 of C2 bytes, a cache of size C serving a fraction C/W of accesses. Simplified: ignores associativity, prefetching and TLB misses.

blocks.title: Cost per access vs working set (simplified model)

scenes.caption: With a 32 KB L1 and 1 MB L2, a 16 KB table costs 3 cycles per access, a 256 KB table 12.6 and a 4 MB table 183. Same code, about 60 times slower, purely from size.
Grow the L2 to 4 MB: the cliff moves right. A benchmark tuned on one machine can sit on the flat part there and on the cliff on your production CPU.
Back to 1 MB L2. A benchmark that tests only one input size picks one point on this curve, usually the cheapest, because test inputs tend to be small.

blocks.prompt: You benchmark a lookup into an 8 KB table, 1000 lookups per iteration. In production the table is touched once per request, after other work has evicted it from every cache. Using the model's costs, how far off is the benchmark?
blocks.reveal: Warm: 1000 x 3 = 3000 cycles. Cold, if every lookup misses to DRAM: 1000 x 240 = 240000 cycles, **80 times** more. Reality lands between the two (lookups that share a cache line hit after the first miss, and the hardware overlaps independent misses), but the warm benchmark can be off by an order of magnitude.

blocks.md:
Ways to measure the case you care about:

- **Sweep sizes.** Register the benchmark over a range of input sizes (`->Range(8, 8<<20)` in Google Benchmark) and plot the result, so you see the cliffs.
- **Make it cold on purpose.** Touch a buffer larger than the last-level cache between iterations. Do that eviction under `state.PauseTiming()`, but note the guide says pausing every iteration is "not recommended, since it has high overhead": batch many operations per pause or subtract a measured baseline.
- **Use realistic inputs.** Random keys, not the same key every time; real string lengths, not one.

Warm-up cuts the other way. The first iterations pay one-time costs: page faults on first touch of new memory, cold instruction caches, and in Java the JIT compiling the method. In the ten repetitions of lesson 2's correct benchmark shown in the next lesson, the first took 3.27 ns and the other nine 3.03 to 3.08 ns. Google Benchmark's `--benchmark_min_warmup_time` runs and discards iterations first; its default is 0 seconds, so warm-up is off unless you ask.

Misconception: "warm-up makes a benchmark more accurate". It makes it measure **steady state**. If your function really runs once per request on cold caches, the warmed number is precise and wrong. Decide which regime production is in, then measure that one.
A microbenchmark's working set and access pattern are part of the experiment. Report them next to the time, and sweep the size if the code's data can be large.

blocks.question: A new hash map is 2x faster than the old one in a benchmark with 1000 keys, but the service using 50 million keys sees no gain. What is the most plausible reason?
options: The benchmark forgot DoNotOptimize
At 1000 keys both maps fit in cache, so the benchmark measured hashing and probing on hot data; at 50 million keys both are dominated by cache misses to DRAM
The service has more threads
Hash maps are O(1), so size cannot matter
blocks.explain: A small key set keeps the whole table in L1 or L2, where instruction counts dominate. A huge table makes nearly every probe a DRAM miss, and a design that saves instructions but makes as many misses gains little. Big-O hides exactly this constant. Sweep the size before trusting the 2x.

blocks.question: Which setup best measures a function that in production runs once per request on cold data?
options: Many iterations on one small input with a long warm-up
Many iterations, each preceded (outside the timed region) by touching a buffer larger than the last-level cache, with batching to amortize pause overhead
One iteration, measured once
Many iterations on a single input with ASLR disabled
blocks.explain: Evicting the caches before each timed call recreates the cold state, and batching keeps the PauseTiming overhead small relative to the work. A long warm-up measures the hot case. A single run is dominated by noise and timer overhead. ASLR affects layout, not cache warmth.

lessons.title: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real

blocks.md:
Run the same correct benchmark twice and you get two different numbers. Google Benchmark's variance guide lists the usual sources: cores that run at different speeds, turbo and boost clocks that change frequency even under the Linux `performance` governor, context switches and other programs on the same CPU, a hyperthread sibling (SMT) sharing the core, cache effects from code on other cores, and NUMA.

Two jobs follow: shrink the noise, then measure what is left and decide with statistics rather than by eye.

blocks.code:
sudo cpupower frequency-set --governor performance   # fixed governor
echo 0 | sudo tee /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/boost  # no boost
taskset -c 2 ./bench --benchmark_repetitions=10          # pin to one CPU
setarch $(uname -m) -R ./bench                          # run without ASLR
blocks.caption: Linux commands from Google Benchmark's reducing-variance guide (run as root where noted). The boost file path depends on the cpufreq driver; LLVM's guide uses intel_pstate/no_turbo on Intel.

scenes.caption: Sequential: four runs of A, then four of B. At 8 s the chip gets hot and lowers its clock. Every B run lands in the slow period, so B looks slower even if A and B are identical.

Interleaved in a random order: each version gets about half its runs in each period, so the slowdown becomes noise shared by both, instead of a bias against B. Google Benchmark offers this as --benchmark_enable_random_interleaving.

blocks.md: Now the statistics. Georges, Buytaert and Eeckhout surveyed Java papers and found that many report the best (fastest) of N runs or a bare mean, and showed that such methods "can be misleading, and can even lead to incorrect conclusions". Their recommendation: take several independent measurements and report the mean with a **confidence interval**, a range that, at a 95% confidence level, is built so that it contains the true mean in 95% of experiments.

blocks.caption: Mean of n runs plus or minus the half-width; s is the sample standard deviation and t comes from Student's t distribution (2.262 for n = 10).

blocks.title: Ten repetitions of three benchmarks (measured, ns)

scenes.caption: Lesson 2's compute, 10 interleaved runs of 20 million iterations each. A divides by the constant 42, which clang turns into multiply and shift. A copy is identical code under another name. B divides by a runtime k: a real divide.
A's first run, 3.27, is the warm-up outlier from lesson 3. Its mean is 3.067 ns with s = 0.073, so the 95% interval is 3.067 plus or minus 0.052: [3.015, 3.119].
A copy: mean 3.051, interval [3.026, 3.076]. It overlaps A's interval almost entirely: no evidence of any difference, as expected for identical code.
B: mean 5.576, interval [5.529, 5.622]. Far from A's interval: B is clearly slower, about 1.82 times A. A real divide costs more than multiply-and-shift.
Best of 10 would say A copy (3.0131) beats A (3.0255) by 0.4%, a confident-looking result for two identical functions. The minimum picks one lucky run and hides the spread.

blocks.title: Interval half-width shrinks like one over root n

scenes.caption: With A's spread (s about 0.07 ns), 10 runs give about plus or minus 0.04 ns. Normal approximation (1.96 instead of t), slightly narrow for small n.
Halving the noise halves the interval. Quadrupling n only halves it too: reducing noise at the source is usually cheaper than adding runs.

blocks.md: Misconception: "overlapping intervals prove the versions are equal". They show you could not detect a difference at this noise level. A smaller real difference may exist; to find it, reduce noise or take more runs.
Repeat, interleave, and report the mean with a confidence interval (or a median with its spread). Never decide from one run or from the best of N.

blocks.question: Version X averages 102 ns with 95% interval [98, 106]. Version Y averages 100 ns with interval [97, 103]. What should you conclude?
options: Y is 2% faster; ship it
The data do not show a difference; reduce noise or take more runs before deciding
X is faster because its interval is wider
Compare the fastest runs instead
blocks.explain: The intervals overlap heavily, so a 2 ns gap is within what noise produces. Width says how uncertain the mean is, not which version is faster. The best-of approach is the misleading method that Georges et al. warn against.

blocks.question: You run 10 repetitions of A, then 10 of B. B's interval is entirely above A's. What hidden flaw could still make the comparison wrong?
options: Ten runs are too few for any interval
A systematic change during the session (thermal throttling, a background job starting) hits only B; interleaving would expose it
Confidence intervals only work for Java
The t value should be 1.96
blocks.explain: An interval measures random scatter, not drift that correlates with the order of runs. Randomly interleaving A and B turns such drift into shared noise. Ten runs are enough to build an interval, and t = 2.262 is correct for n = 10.

lessons.title: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles

blocks.md: Low noise is not the end. LLVM's benchmarking guide puts it plainly: "low noise is required, but not sufficient. It does not exclude measurement bias." **Measurement bias** is a systematic error: something in the setup that consistently favors one version, so repeating the run gives the same wrong answer with a tight confidence interval.

Mytkowicz, Diwan, Hauswirth and Sweeney (ASPLOS 2009) measured the speedup of gcc's `-O3` over `-O2` on SPEC CPU2006 while changing two things that look irrelevant:

- **UNIX environment size**: the bytes of environment variables. The environment is loaded into memory just before the call stack, so its size shifts the stack's start address and the alignment of every local variable.
- **Link order**: the order of `.o` files given to the linker, which shifts code and data addresses.

Caches, branch predictors and hardware that detects conflicts between loads and stores all depend on addresses, so these shifts change speed.

blocks.title: Speedup of -O3 over -O2 depends on the setup

scenes.caption: Core 2, perlbench, 33 link orders. One order gives 0.92: -O3 looks slower than -O2. Values above 1 mean -O3 is faster.
Same program, same compiler flags, a different link order: 1.10, a 10% speedup. Each point was 5 runs with tight 95% intervals, so this is reproducible behavior, not noise.
Changing only the size of an unused environment variable, lbm on Core 2 ranged from 0.88 (a clear slowdown) to 1.09 (a healthy speedup).

Their fix, setup randomization: measure across many random link orders and environment sizes and summarize the distribution. For perlbench that gives 1.007 plus or minus 0.003 at 95% confidence: a tiny real effect.

blocks.md:
Curtsinger and Berger's **Stabilizer** (ASPLOS 2013) automates this. It randomizes the placement of code, stack frames and heap objects, and re-randomizes during the run (every 500 ms by default), so each run samples many layouts. That makes the layout effect behave like random noise that statistical tests can account for. Evaluating LLVM on SPEC CPU2006 this way, they found -O2 significantly faster than -O1, but the effect of -O3 over -O2 "indistinguishable from random noise".

The lesson for a microbenchmark: a 2% win from a change that also moves code around may be a layout accident. Check it in other builds, other link orders, or other machines before believing it.

Managed runtimes add their own bias. A JIT compiler optimizes using a **profile** of what it has seen so far, such as which classes a call site has received. JMH's forking sample defines two identical `Counter` classes and runs them in one JVM: Counter1 alone is fast, Counter2 is slower, and then Counter1 is slow again, because the shared call site's profile now mixes both classes. Each benchmark inherits the history of the ones before it. JMH's fix is to run each benchmark in a fresh JVM (a **fork**), which it does by default.

blocks.title: JIT profile pollution and the fork fix

scenes.caption: Fork(0): all three benchmarks share one JVM. The first one sees only Counter1 at the call site, and the JIT specializes the code for it.
The second benchmark sends Counter2 through the same call site. The profile now holds two classes and the code is recompiled for both: slower.

labels.site:
call site c.inc()
seen: Counter1, Counter2

scenes.caption: Counter1 again, identical code to the first run, is now slow too, because the profile still contains Counter2. Run order changed the result.

labels.site:
call site c.inc()
seen: Counter1, Counter2

scenes.caption: With forking (JMH forks by default, 5 forks unless set; the sample uses Fork(1)), each benchmark runs in a fresh JVM with an empty profile, so none can pollute another.

labels.site:
call site c.inc()
seen: own class only

blocks.prompt: You reorder two functions in a source file, change nothing else, and a microbenchmark of one of them gets 4% faster with a tight confidence interval on a quiet, pinned machine. Is the reorder an optimization?
blocks.reveal: Probably not one you can rely on. Moving code changes addresses and alignment, which Mytkowicz et al. showed can swing results by several percent in either direction, reproducibly. Re-test under different link orders or environment sizes, or with a layout randomizer such as Stabilizer. If the gain survives randomization, it is real; if it flips sign, it was layout luck.

blocks.md: Misconception: "disabling ASLR and pinning the CPU makes my benchmark correct". They reduce run-to-run noise, which narrows intervals. A narrow interval around a biased setup is a confidently wrong answer.
Noise you can see and average away; bias you cannot. Vary the setup (layout, link order, process, machine) and trust only effects that survive the variation.

blocks.question: In a JMH run with forks set to 0, benchmark C is 30% slower when it runs after benchmark D than when it runs alone. What is the right fix?
options: Increase warm-up iterations so the JIT settles
Run each benchmark in its own forked JVM, as JMH does by default
Disable ASLR
Add a Blackhole to benchmark C
blocks.explain: C inherits JIT profiles from D in a shared JVM, the effect JMHSample_12_Forking demonstrates. More warm-up in the same JVM keeps the polluted profile. ASLR and Blackholes address layout noise and dead code, which are not the problem here.

blocks.question: Mytkowicz et al. found that link order alone moved perlbench's -O3 speedup between 0.92 and 1.10. What does that imply for a single-build comparison of two compiler flags?
options: Only that more repetitions are needed
A single build is one sample of memory layout, so its result can favor either flag regardless of how many times it is run
Link order matters only for programs as large as perlbench
The Core 2 was faulty
blocks.explain: Each point in their data was reproducible across runs, so repetitions do not help: the bias is fixed by the build's layout. Stabilizer's authors put it directly: a single binary is one sample from the space of program layouts. Mytkowicz et al. saw such effects on every machine they tried, including a simulator.
